items.full: WooCommerce is the open-source ecommerce platform for WordPress. Our core platform is free, flexible, and amplified by a global community. The freedom of open-source means you retain full ownership of your store’s content and data forever. Whether you’re launching a business, taking brick-and-mortar retail online, or developing sites for clients, use WooCommerce for a store that powerfully blends content and commerce. Built-in tools and popular integrations help you efficiently manage your business operations. Many services are free to add with a single click via the optional Setup Wizard . WooCommerce means business. Keep tabs on the performance metrics most important to you with a powerful and flexible central dashboard built into WooCommerce. Expand your audience across marketing and social channels with Google Ads , HubSpot , Mailchimp , and Facebook integrations. You can always check out the in-dashboard Marketing Hub for fresh ideas and tips to help you succeed. Our developers vet each new extension and regularly review existing extensions to maintain Marketplace quality standards. Unlike hosted ecommerce solutions, WooCommerce store data is future-proof; you’re free to export all your content and take your site to any platform you choose. No restrictions. Developers can use WooCommerce to create, customize, and scale a store to meet a client’s exact specifications, making enhancements through extensions or custom solutions. The core platform is tested rigorously and often, supported by a dedicated development team working across time zones. Comprehensive documentation is updated with each release, empowering you to build exactly the store required. WooCommerce has a large, passionate community dedicated to helping merchants succeed – and it’s growing fast. There are WooCommerce Meetups in locations around the world that you can attend for free and even get involved in running. These events are a great way to learn from others, share your expertise, and connect with like-minded folks. WooCommerce also has a regular presence at WordCamps across the globe – we’d love to meet you. WooCommerce is developed and supported by Automattic, the creators of WordPress.com and Jetpack. We also have hundreds of independent contributors, and there’s always room for more. Head to the WooCommerce GitHub Repository to find out how you can pitch in. items.title: Schools that turn off Google's AI will lose search too starting in 2027
items.desc: Starting in 2027, Google plans to turn off AI features in its school products by default, letting schools decide what to enable. The catch: schools that block AI entirely on their devices will also lose access to Google Search, since the two systems are now too deeply intertwined to separate. Given Google's grip on the US school market, that "choice" doesn't leave schools with much room to maneuver. The article Schools that turn off Google's AI will lose search too starting in 2027 appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Starting in early 2027, Google will give schools an ultimatum: accept AI for students or lose access to Google Search entirely. Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Google Search will all be off by default for student accounts. Schools can turn each one on individually. But a version of search without AI? That's no longer on the table. The New York Times broke the story first. Google's vice president for education, Chris Phillips, said search and AI have become too tightly fused to pull apart. Google recently flipped AI features on by default inside its learning platform Classroom for schools with Gemini access. That move drew backlash, and the company is now reversing course. Schools that choose to enable search will get two flavors: search with full AI overviews and AI chat, or search with "Guided Learning," a mode designed to steer students toward answers rather than hand them over directly. None of this happens in a vacuum. Google dominates the US school market with Chromebooks, Gmail, and Classroom. Education professor Morgan Polikoff called the move a textbook case of the tech industry shoving AI onto people whether they want it or not. The country's two largest school districts, New York City and Los Angeles, had already pulled back on AI for students in September. Los Angeles specifically wanted to keep using Google Search without AI overviews. Google won't let them. items.title: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
items.desc: Called FlashProve, the system would let anyone check that an AI response really came from the model it claims to be from.
items.full: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Image Credits: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto / Getty Images AI Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity Russell Brandom 2:41 PM PST · November 3, 2026 Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday. The system, called FlashProve , is built to provide what researchers call “provable inference” — a cryptographic proof, essentially a mathematical guarantee, that a given output came from a specific model. It’s meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they’re using. Similar to cryptographic email signatures that let recipients confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, FlashProve would be robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model. In particular, the researchers note that the system could be used to prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results. FlashProve could also be used to verify claims by third parties that a specific task was done by an advanced model. “A developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model,” the researchers write. “How can a user verify these claims?” To work, the system requires AI labs to publish a “fingerprint” of each model they release that can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically. Crucially, the fingerprints don’t reveal a model’s weights, the internal numbers that define how it behaves and which closed-model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. That means labs could publish the fingerprints without giving up their most valuable asset, enabling the system to work with commercial models, too. The system is also designed to be lightweight, so verification could be performed on a local device. As part of the announcement, researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code for various elements of the system, which is publicly available under an open source license on GitHub . Research in the system is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab. “This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda,” researchers explain in the announcement post. “We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . ChatGPT can now turn text prompts and photos into animated GIFs with OpenAI's Images 2.6 model
items.desc: OpenAI is adding a GIF feature to ChatGPT. With the new Images 2.6 model, users can create animated GIFs from text prompts or photos and then adjust speed and individual frames. The model's image consistency is strong enough to keep characters recognizable across frames, making flipbook-style animation possible. According to OpenAI, users now generate more than four billion images per week. The article ChatGPT can now turn text prompts and photos into animated GIFs with OpenAI's Images 2.6 model appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: ChatGPT can now create animated GIFs. The update is based on OpenAI's new Images 2.6 model and is rolling out to all ChatGPT and Codex users on web, desktop, and mobile apps, The Verge reports. Users can generate a GIF from a text prompt or uploaded photo, then adjust animation speed or edit individual frames. As an example, OpenAI showed how the prompt "Can you make a gif of a cat dancing?" produces several slight variations of a character that are strung together flipbook-style into a GIF. The model's image consistency appears strong enough to keep the character recognizable across frames, while earlier models would likely have altered its look too much from one frame to the next for the trick to work. Beyond GIFs, Images 2.6 is also meant to speed up image generation overall. For developers, OpenAI is also releasing the API models GPT-Image-2.6 "Flare" for efficient and "Sunburst" for higher-quality image generation. Both model variants were first introduced with Image 2.5 . OpeneAI says users now generate well over four billion images per week via ChatGPT and the API, one billion more than in September. items.title: Anthropic's text watermark is easy to bypass on several older Claude models
items.desc: Anthropic is rolling out text watermarks to four more Claude models ahead of the EU AI Act's December deadline. But on older models like Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6, API users can disable the watermark by changing a single sampling parameter. Anthropic's response to the loophole? A compliance warning. The article Anthropic's text watermark is easy to bypass on several older Claude models appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Update, November 4, 2026: Anthropic emailed API customers again about a second round of watermark retrofits. Starting November 16, 2026, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Claude Haiku 4.5 will all get text watermarking. On Amazon Bedrock, the rollout may take a few extra days. Claude Opus 4.6 was originally part of the first wave and should have gotten the watermark on November 3. Anthropic explicitly confirms the delay to November 16 but gives no reason. The other three first-wave models, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, don't show up in the new email so their rollout likely went ahead on November 3 as planned. Ad Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Claude Haiku 4.5 are three models that weren't part of the previous announcement. All four models in this wave share the same sampling restriction: the watermark only applies when temperature , top_p , and top_k are set to their defaults. In the first wave, that limit only hit two of four models (Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6). Ad Original article, October 31, 2026: Anthropic is expanding its text watermark to four more Claude models, but API users can dodge the mark on two of them by tweaking a single sampling parameter. Ad In an email to API customers, Anthropic said it will watermark Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Newer models like Claude Opus 5.5 already carry the mark, and the rollout on Amazon Bedrock may take a few extra days. Anthropic calls the watermark an "imperceptible pattern in word choice" that doesn't change meaning, quality, or readability. The company says it adds no extra characters or tokens, doesn't affect pricing or request and response formats, and barely slows output speed. Anthropic also says the watermark "contains no information about the user, their organization, or their conversations with Claude." Ad On Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, Anthropic says the watermark kicks in only when developers leave the three sampling parameters at their default values. Those parameters, temperature , top_p , and top_k , control how much randomness the model uses when picking words. A minor tweak to any one of them is enough to dodge the watermark. Anthropic warns in its email that "If you rely on the watermark for your own compliance, keep these settings at their defaults." Ad The email doesn't mention that caveat for Claude Mythos 5 or Claude Opus 4.7, which suggests the watermark applies to those models regardless of sampling settings. But the loophole on the older models is still notable, since Opus 4.6 remains Anthropic's best writing model , ahead of even Opus 5.5. Anthropic has a detection API in private preview for verifying the watermark and offers more details on its content labeling information page . Anthropic points to the EU AI Act's December deadline as the reason it's watermarking older models now. Every model released after Aug. 2, 2026, shipped with the watermark on day one, while older models are getting it in stages. Combined with OpenAI's recently launched Git backend Pando, the deal shows the company is building out its infrastructure for developers and AI agents working side by side. The article OpenAI acquires Pierre Computer Company to make Git keep up with AI coding agents appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI is buying Pierre Computer Company, Inc., the startup behind Code Storage and several open-source tools. Pierre's libraries already power OpenAI's coding agent Codex. "Trees" handles fast project file navigation, "Diffs" displays code changes and lets users fix bugs right in the diff view, and "Highlights" is a real-time syntax highlighter that works as developers type or an AI agent generates code. Code Storage stores code and tracks history through Git. OpenAI says the acquisition is about making Git workflows work better when developers and AI agents are writing code side by side. As agents handle more tasks in parallel, the tooling around Git has to keep up. OpenAI already runs Pando , its own version control backend built for both developers and agents. Pierre's open-source projects will stay open source. The deal still needs regulatory approval. items.title: PCrisk Trust Badge Review: A Verifiable Security Badge for WordPress
items.desc: High-reputation websites need to display trust credentials. My PCrisk Trust Badge review covers a solution that helps you achieve this with ease through displaying a dynamic (and customizable) badge. The post " PCrisk Trust Badge Review: A Verifiable Security Badge for WordPress " first appeared on WP Mayor .
items.full: Any website that relies on trust to facilitate sales needs to showcase that wherever customers show up. I’ve got a PCrisk Trust Badge review today that gives you a near-perfect solution! It makes regular scans of your site for malware and other malicious intent, then displays a badge if all is well. However, if something comes up in the scan, the badge will hide again until you resolve it. The premise is simple, but this review will help you decide whether its application is also straightforward. Spoiler alert: I think it’s an easy decision to make! I’ll start with the three premium plans and give you the lowdown on the free version after. Note that the prices here are for month-by-month billing and annual plans come with two months free usage: As for the free version, PCrisk will scan one site, once per month, then sends you the results complete with a trust score and summary. None of the premium functionality is available in the free version. I’m going to talk more about the use cases shortly. However, in short, the Solo plan is ideal for a single store. If you run an agency, Pro would suit you. The Business plan would also work for an agency with a larger portfolio, or if you know that portfolio will grow in the future. PCrisk Trust Badge is also available as a Shopify app and as a script snippet for any other website platform, but the focus is (of course) on the WordPress plugin for this review. WordPress security plugins do a huge service to millions of sites. In my opinion, they’re likely the hardest working plugins you’ll install. However, the public never sees any of this. In some cases, the website will display a static seal or badge to indicate that the site has security. PCrisk Trust Badge displays a dynamic badge. This links to a public report that shows details such as the scan date, a trust score, and the engines it used. If a scan fails, the badge won’t show. The scan itself covers a few areas: Malware, phishing feeds, obfuscated scripts, SSL validity, and more. However, your current WordPress security plugin still has a vital part to play as PCrisk Trust Badge only detects and reports on issues. Agency owners will love the peace of mind this gives to clients. In fact, anyone who runs multiple sites will find value in the plugin. So will WooCommerce stores, small businesses or lead-generation websites. Anywhere customers need to know your site is safe to pass their data through will find benefits in PCrisk Trust Badge. The core of PCrisk Trust Badge is its scanning: daily for premium plans and monthly for the free plan. Scans run on PCrisk’s servers, so there’s no load on your site. There’s no impact on page speeds for the free version as the plugin adds nothing to public pages. It’s worth noting that PCrisk Trust Badge aims to respect data privacy. It’s a ‘cookie-free’ solution, although it does load an external script and contacts PCrisk servers. However, you have to explicitly approve those connections with WordPress. Visitors won’t see a different experience than usual, but requests do send an IP address and the page URL to PCrisk. The dynamic badge is a unique element. items.title: Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible
items.desc: As LLM chat patterns become more widespread, making them accessible is essential to ensuring everyone can access the information, tools, and opportunities they offer. Drawing on his work improving these interfaces, Eric Bailey shares practical ways to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who rely on assistive technology.
items.full: About The Author Eric is a Boston-based designer who helps create straightforward solutions that address a person’s practical, physical, cognitive, and emotional needs. More about Eric ↬ Weekly tips on front-end & UX . Trusted by 182,000+ folks. Design Patterns For AI Interfaces with Vitaly Friedman Designing For Complex UI Masterclass with Vitaly Friedman Meet AI 2027 Conference, December 1, 2026. Building Modern HTML Emails with Rémi Parmentier As LLM chat patterns become more widespread, making them accessible is essential to ensuring everyone can access the information, tools, and opportunities they offer. Drawing on his work improving these interfaces, Eric Bailey shares practical ways to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who rely on assistive technology. I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career. Now I want to share this knowledge with you. Accessibility is a core part of a functional digital experience. As the LLM chat pattern continues to spread like wildfire across the web, we risk excluding people if these experiences are not built with accessibility as a core consideration. It is also worth re-mentioning what “exclusion” means here : It’s the loss of knowledge, the loss of opportunity, the loss of utility, the loss of employability, the loss of entertainment, and more. “Immersive LLM chat experience” is a catch-all term for full-screen experiences like Claude , ChatGPT , GitHub Copilot , Gemini , America.gov , Glean , and other similar websites and web apps: The majority of what this post covers applies to both web apps and native apps . This is because these experiences are typically built using web technologies, then placed in a native wrapper via frameworks such as Electron or Tauri . Immersive LLM chat experiences are not patterns such as a pop-up chat, inline text generation utilities, or summarization tools. These simpler applications of LLM technology will have different considerations and expectations. Instead, this is a starting point for making those other experiences accessible. There is nothing special about chat-based UIs when viewed via the lens of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines . They are interactive experiences, built using web technologies. The losses I’ve described — and the legal liability associated with them — are access barriers in the same way any other web content can be an access barrier. I would also like to mention the social model of disability here: the idea that exclusion can be created by the built environment. For example, consider an elevated entryway that uses a gently sloping ramp in place of stairs. Built environments also extend to digital experiences , and the social model also applies here. The main activities undertaken to operate an LLM chat are already well-established: It is how we facilitate — or fail to facilitate — those interactions that’s the salient bit. items.title: From reading to acting: WebMCP and the agent-ready web
items.desc: From reading to acting: see how WebMCP could make your site agent-ready, where it falls short, and how to try it on your own site.
items.full: Loading... In my last post , most of the approaches I covered for making sites agent ready were about helping agents read a site. MCP servers (which are not the same as WebMCP despite the confusingly similar name) let agents act too, but only for people who connect the server to their AI assistant, which is a big ask. For everyone else, an agent that needs to submit a form, book a time, or add something to a cart still has to find the parts of the page made for people and type into them, which often fails. I wrapped up by saying we’d look at WebMCP next, which aims to let any visitor’s agent use a site’s forms and actions directly in the browser, without having to install or connect anything extra. By the way, if you’re new to this series on agent readiness, the first post covers what agent-ready means. WebMCP is a way for a website to tell the AI agent in your browser what it can do on the page, and how. Today, if you ask your AI assistant to send a message through a site’s contact form, it has to look at the page the way a person would, find the right fields, and type into them. With WebMCP, the site offers the agent a short list of clear actions, like “send a message” or “search products,” each with a description of what it does and what information it needs. WebMCP calls these actions “tools.” The agent picks the tool it needs and fills in the details, and the site’s own code does the rest. WebMCP already works in Chrome and Edge, though it’s still being tested. Chrome opened an origin trial in Chrome 149, and Edge is running one too. That means the feature works for real visitors, but only on sites that sign up and add a trial token to their pages, and only while the trial runs. Even this early, Google is already looking at WebMCP as part of a healthy site: Lighthouse now checks to see if a page has WebMCP tools, and whether its forms are marked up for them. WebMCP’s big advantage is that it brings the act side of agent readiness seamlessly into the browser, which is great because everyone already knows how to use a browser. It works inside the user’s tab and with their login, so there’s no separate server to build, no OAuth flow, and nothing extra to install or connect. This simplicity gives WebMCP an advantage over MCP. WebMCP not only works inside the browser you already have, it also reuses what sites have built. Tools can be applied to a site’s existing search, cart, and form code with a few lines of JavaScript, or set up in the HTML by just adding two attributes to a form. In WordPress, where most forms come from a handful of plugins, one plugin update could turn millions of forms into tools. Elementor is a good example of that: we’re planning WebMCP support for actions in our Atomic Elements, starting with Atomic Forms, as we announced with the Elementor 4.4 beta . Yet again, WordPress proves itself to be agent ready , because it already has much of the groundwork in place for WebMCP. The Abilities API , added in WordPress 6.9, gives WordPress, plugins, and themes one place to declare what they can do: each ability has a name, a description, a schema for its inputs and outputs, and a permission check tied to WordPress’s own user r

items.title: Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset
items.desc: Stu created tidy-typography.css: a style reset for taming typography with modern CSS features for everything from fluid typography and vertical rhythm, to hyphens and variable fonts. Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset . text-wrap: pretty can prevent a stranded word, container query units can scale a heading to the column it occupies, and text-box can trim the half-leading built into a line box. Some of these features are experimental and browser support is uneven, so they need guardrails rather than blind inclusion. I’ve put together tidy-typography.css , which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail. Use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you. I’ll walk you through all the details in this article and give you the full code at the end. Rendering and fallback sanity html { -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased; text-rendering: optimizeLegibility; font-synthesis: none; -moz-text-size-adjust: none; -webkit-text-size-adjust: none; text-size-adjust: none; } body { font-size-adjust: from-font; } font-synthesis: none stops a browser from inventing bold or italic when the family lacks that face. The smoothing and text-rendering declarations are rendering hints, mainly for WebKit; results still vary by platform. text-size-adjust disables mobile font inflation that can make a deliberately sized layout jump on rotation. font-size-adjust: from-font uses font metrics to reduce the apparent size change while a fallback swaps for a webfont. (As with other snippets in this article, this ⁠ :root block is a partial excerpt the final stylesheet combines it with additional custom properties defined later on.) Fluid typography Viewport-based fluid type does not know how wide its element is. A heading in a narrow sidebar can therefore scale as though it fills the viewport. .article-container { container-type: inline-size; } :root { --step-0: clamp(1rem, 0.9rem + 1cqi, 1.125rem); --step-3: clamp(2rem, 1.6rem + 3cqi, 2.75rem); } container-type: inline-size makes the wrapper a container query , so its children can use cqi : a unit based on the container rather than the viewport. Replacing vw in clamp() lets the same heading scale appropriately in an article column or a 300px sidebar without component-specific media queries. Vertical rhythm: trim the half-leading :heading, p, blockquote, figcaption, li { text-box-trim: trim-both; text-box-edge: cap alphabetic; /* shorthand: text-box: trim-both cap alphabetic; */ } line-height includes space above the cap-height and below the baseline: half-leading. It becomes obvious when text must align tightly with another element. text-box-trim removes it, while text-box-edge measures from capital-letter caps to the alphabetic baseline. This is a metrics-aware alternative to font-specific negative-margin nudges. @supports selector(:heading) { :heading { text-box: trim-both cap alphabetic; } } Selectors Level 5 proposes :heading , matching h1 to h6 and [role="heading"] . It has not landed in browsers, so keep it behind an @supports selector() check. Balanced headlines, orphan-free paragraphs :heading, blockquote, figcaption { text-wrap: balance; } p, li, dd

items.title: Welcome Drip and Sleeknote to the WPBeginner Family of Products
items.desc: Today, I’m extremely excited to share that Drip and Sleeknote are joining the Awesome Motive network, and they’re now part of the WPBeginner family of products. Drip is an email marketing and automation platform designed for small businesses, from content creators to online stores. More…
items.full: Today, I’m extremely excited to share that Drip and Sleeknote are joining the Awesome Motive network, and they’re now part of the WPBeginner family of products . Drip is an email marketing and automation platform designed for small businesses, from content creators to online stores. More than 6,000 brands use Drip to turn first-time visitors into subscribers, buyers, and repeat customers. On the other hand, Sleeknote is a conversion optimization tool that turns your website visitors into subscribers and customers with popups, slide-ins, sticky bars, and more. Together, Sleeknote and Drip help you drive more conversions by reaching customers wherever they engage with your brand, whether that’s on your website, in their email inbox, or through SMS. Drip gives small businesses and ecommerce store owners everything they need to grow sales with email, without the high costs. It works with WooCommerce, Shopify, and BigCommerce. That means your store data flows straight into your email marketing tool, so you can personalize your messages based on what your customers actually do and buy. We’ve been using Drip to power the email marketing on WPBeginner and our product brands for many years, so I’ve seen firsthand how much revenue a good email setup can bring in. Sleeknote helps you get more email signups and sales from the traffic you already have. You can control exactly who sees each campaign and when. For example, you can target visitors based on the pages they view, where they came from, whether they’re new or returning, and what’s in their cart, so every message feels relevant instead of random. Sleeknote is free for all users on Drip as part of the Drip forms. Let’s take a detailed look. Drip comes with a drag-and-drop visual workflow builder. You can use it to create anything from a single automated email to a complex multi-step campaign. You don’t have to start from scratch, either. You can choose from Drip’s extensive ready-made workflow templates and install them on your account with a single click. You can easily customize each workflow by adding decisions, delays, and goals to guide subscribers along the right path. You can even split-test different paths to see which ones generate more revenue. Drip comes with a free MCP connector on every plan. It lets you connect AI assistants like Claude or ChatGPT directly to your Drip account. Simply put, you can ask your AI which campaign made the most money last month or have it draft and schedule your next campaign. Some messages work better as a text than an email, like a flash sale that ends tonight or a cart a shopper left a few minutes ago. Drip now has built-in SMS marketing for stores in the United States (other countries coming soon). You can run your email and text campaigns from the same account, using the same customer data and segments. You can send one-off text campaigns to any segment, or add SMS steps to your workflows. For example, your abandoned cart workflow can send a reminder email first, then follow up with a text if the shopper still hasn’t checked out. The SMS builder counts your characters as you type, lets you personalize each message, and adds the required opt-out language

items.title: Infinite Uploads 3.5 Adds a Free Plan, Media Cleanup, and Secure File Downloads
items.desc: Infinite Uploads now lets agencies test WordPress media offload on a client site for free, with no credit card and no time limit. It also adds Media Cleanup, which shows you which files look unused or duplicated before you delete anything, along with signed links that protect the files you sell through WooCommerce and Easy Digital Downloads. The post " Infinite Uploads 3.5 Adds a Free Plan, Media Cleanup, and Secure File Downloads " first appeared on WP Mayor .
items.full: If you’ve ever wanted to try WordPress media offload on a client site without getting a credit card out, Infinite Uploads 3.5 now lets you do that. It also brings WordPress media cleanup, so you can see which files nothing seems to be using, along with protection for the files you sell through WooCommerce and Easy Digital Downloads. Our own media library at WP Mayor has over 25,000 files in it, so I know how quickly these things get out of hand. I’d imagine plenty of your client sites are the same, with old logos and campaign graphics that nobody wants to touch in case something breaks. Here’s what’s new and what it means if you’re looking after sites for clients. The new Free Infinite Uploads plan gives you 10 GB of cloud storage and 20 GB of CDN bandwidth a month, shared across all the sites on your account. You don’t need a credit card and there’s no time limit, so you can leave it running on a client site for as long as it stays within those allowances. I also like how they’ve dealt with the limits. If a Free site runs out of storage, new uploads pause and you get a message explaining why. A sync that wouldn’t fit won’t start at all, so you’re not left with half a library in the cloud. When a site outgrows the plan, you can upgrade and your files stay where they are. Just keep in mind that a Free site that stops checking in for 90 days gets archived and its files deleted, although you’ll get two warning emails first. You’ll need a Business plan for Media Cleanup, image optimization and protected downloads. If you’d like to try those before paying, I’d go straight for the 7-day trial on a Business plan, because upgrading from Free starts your billing right away. Our Infinite Uploads review has more on how offloading works. Media Cleanup scans your library and marks each file as In use, Possibly unused or Unknown. You’ll see Unknown when the scan can’t rule something out, like a PDF you’ve linked to from an email. It checks a lot more than post content, too. The scan looks through Elementor, Beaver Builder, Divi, Bricks and Oxygen layouts, WooCommerce products and categories, ACF fields, widgets and theme settings, and then loads your public pages the way a visitor would. You can hover over any file to see what’s using it before you make a decision. I’d start with the Possibly unused list sorted by size, since that puts your biggest files at the top. Possible duplicates get grouped together too, so you can compare all those copies of the same team photo side by side and check whether they match byte for byte. If you’re doing this for a client, the CSV export gives you a list to send over for sign-off. Media Cleanup won’t delete anything for you, so you’ll still remove files yourself from Media > Library once you’re sure. It’s included with Business plans and only administrators can use it. Once you’ve switched it on in the Infinite Uploads settings, you’ll find it under Media > Media Cleanup , so you can clean up your library in the same plugin you use for its folders, sorting and search . If you sell digital products and keep the files in the cloud, this one’s worth knowing about. Until now, all it took was one customer sharing a file’s UR

items.title: Dive into the Ipsum WordPress theme, and how to extend it
items.desc: With WordPress 7.2 launching in December, a new default theme is on the way. Marking a departure from tradition, it drops the usual calendar-year naming scheme ...
items.full: With WordPress 7.2 launching in December, a new default theme is on the way. Marking a departure from tradition, it drops the usual calendar-year naming scheme in favor of a more meaningful name. Dubbed Ipsum , this new addition is a minimalist, lightweight, and modular block theme built for Full Site Editing (FSE) and strictly aligned with modern Block Editor standards. As the name suggests, Ipsum streamlines the blogging experience and works out of the box the moment you start writing. Its design is understated in every detail, from subtle dotted underlines to the bundled typography and a curated set of style variations , focused on accessibility and readability. Don’t let its minimalist nature fool you, though. Ipsum provides the ideal blank canvas to bring your creative vision as a blogger to life. Let’s dive into the latest default theme and explore how to get the most out of it using native WordPress features. Ipsum features a minimalist design with a strong focus on readability. The new default theme defines six shades of gray with high-contrast combinations alongside a single accent color. The default background ( #fcfcfc ) and body text ( #000000bf ) achieve a contrast ratio (CR) of 10.26:1, easily earning a WCAG AAA rating. Ipsum supports native WordPress keyboard navigation, displaying a “Skip to content” link on every page. This allows users navigating with the Tab key to jump straight to the main content without having to cycle through header navigation links. The theme also highlights focused links with its accent color, letting keyboard users quickly identify the active element. Typography plays a major role in making Ipsum easy on the eyes, offering five preset font sizes and supporting fluid typography . Links are distinguished only by a subtle dotted underline. While aligned with the theme’s minimalist aesthetic, this might make them hard to spot depending on the page’s color conditions. That said, links remain easy to identify during keyboard navigation thanks to the accent-colored focus outline. Now, let’s take a closer look at Ipsum’s specific features. Ipsum includes a built-in set of templates that delegate page layouts to internal patterns. As an example, here is the markup of the page.html template: <!-- wp:pattern {"slug":"ipsum/hidden-page"} /--> This single line of code calls the hidden pattern hidden-page.php , which controls the layout and sets the required metadata: /** * Title: Pages * Slug: ipsum/hidden-page * Template Types: page * Inserter: no * * @package Ipsum * @since Ipsum 1.0 */ The theme registers custom template variants, such as index-sidebar and archive-sidebar , directly via PHP so you can select them in the Site Editor. As of now, roughly 60 patterns are available to help you build and format your content. While some of these patterns are reserved (hidden) for the theme’s core templates, the majority are fully accessible for you to use in your pages. An interesting technical detail for developers is how patterns implement the Block Bindings API . For example, the archive-full.php pattern uses bindings as follows: <!-- wp:paragraph { "metadata":{ "bindings":{ "content":{ "source":"ipsum/comments-ct
